text.summaryCard: The 1940 report of the Bengal Land Revenue Commission (the Floud Commission). It recommended that sharecroppers be treated as tenants and that the landlord's legally recoverable share of the crop fall from half to one-third.

entries.why: The old summary said the report recommended the sharecroppers' share 'rise from one-half to two-thirds'. The report frames it as the landlord's share falling to one-third (para. 146).

add.supports: The 1940 provincial Krishak Sabha conference at Panjia first called on bargadars to campaign for tebhaga.
Panjia, Jessore district, 1940; the conference adopted the demand that bargadars and adhiars take two of three shares.

Dinajpur, Rangpur and Jalpaiguri among the most affected districts.
A seven-day meeting of peasant workers from Dinajpur, Rangpur and Jalpaiguri, led by Bhabani Sen, decided where in Dinajpur the struggle would be fought.

text.fullEntry: Adivasi and Rajbanshi sharecroppers were at the centre of North Bengal's Tebhaga actions. In Dinajpur the organised peasant movement had, since 1936-37, drawn on Rajbanshi, Muslim and Santal cultivators; peasant workers from Dinajpur, Rangpur and Jalpaiguri met for a week under the provincial Kisan Sabha leader Bhabani Sen to decide where the struggle would be fought.

entries.why: The old text's 'over 1,000 acres' figure came only from Grokipedia and is dropped until a source supports it. Malda is named in the summary but not in these sources.

add.supports: Division of produce: seed returned to whoever supplied it; owner and bargadar each one-third of the balance; the last third by contribution to cultivation costs; a bargadar entitled by contract or custom to more keeps it.

text.title: West Bengal Bargadars Act passed
text.summaryCard: In March 1950 the West Bengal Bargadars Act set rules for dividing a sharecropped harvest. It did not grant the two-thirds the movement had demanded: after seed, owner and bargadar each got a third, and the last third was split by what each had put into cultivation.
text.fullEntry: The West Bengal Bargadars Act, 1950 (West Bengal Act II of 1950) laid down how produce was to be divided where owner and bargadar had no written agreement. Whoever supplied the seed first took back an equal quantity of produce. Owner and bargadar were then each entitled to one-third of the balance, and the remaining third was divided 'in such proportion as would be fair and reasonable', according to each side's contribution of plough-cattle, implements, manure and the cost of protecting or irrigating the land. A bargadar entitled to a larger share by contract or local custom kept it. In practice, a bargadar who supplied all the inputs could reach two-thirds, but the Act did not make two-thirds the rule.

entries.why: The old text said the Act 'formally recognised sharecroppers' entitlement to two-thirds of the produce where they supplied the inputs'. Section 3 sets a one-third/one-third/contribution split instead. The two-thirds wording came from exam-prep sites.

Thakurgaon peasant leader; on the first Dinajpur district Communist Party committee; jailed six months over the chowkidari tax campaign; ran village peasant courts; killed in police firing in the Khapra Ward of Rajshahi jail on 24 April 1950.

text.summaryCard: Peasant leader in Thakurgaon, Dinajpur, and one of the first peasant members of the district Communist Party committee. Killed in police firing in the Khapra Ward of Rajshahi jail on 24 April 1950.
text.fullEntry: Kampram Singh led poorer peasants in Thakurgaon against the influence of richer cultivators in the local peasant committee, and became one of two peasant members of the first Dinajpur district committee of the Communist Party. He was jailed for six months in the campaign against the chowkidari tax, and during the Tebhaga movement sat on the village peasant courts that kept order after jotedars fled. On 21 February 1947 armed police came to Thumnia to arrest him and Doma Singh. He was later imprisoned in Rajshahi jail, where he was killed in police firing in the Khapra Ward on 24 April 1950.

entries.why: The old text paired him with 'Bhawan Singh', who cannot be traced (see pe_bhawan_singh). The new text comes from participants' memoirs in Tebhaga Andolan.

add.supports: Released from detention in 1938; one of the founders of the Dinajpur district Communist Party; in charge of the Phulbari and Patiram areas with Rupnarayan Roy; author of the memoir 'Dinajpur jelar krishak andolan: shuru theke tebhaga porjonto' in this collection.
An organiser of the Khanpur struggle; composed a song about Khanpur in Rajshahi Central Jail on 24 April 1950.

text.summaryCard: A Dinajpur revolutionary turned communist who helped found the district Communist Party, led the Tebhaga struggle around Phulbari and Patiram, and later wrote his own account of it.
text.fullEntry: Kali Sarkar came out of detention in 1938 having turned from revolutionary terrorism to Marxism, and with Bibhuti Guha and Sushil Sen formed the Communist Party in Dinajpur district. During the Tebhaga movement he was responsible, with Rupnarayan Roy, for the Phulbari and Patiram areas, and he was among the organisers of the struggle at Khanpur. Imprisoned in Rajshahi Central Jail, he composed a song about Khanpur there. His memoir of the Dinajpur peasant movement from its beginnings to Tebhaga is printed in Dhananjay Ray's collection Tebhaga Andolan.

entries.why: The old text was a placeholder saying his role was not verified.

add.supports: Peasant leader of the Phulbari area; the Krishak Samiti and Communist Party's candidate in the 1946 Legislative Assembly election, which he won against a jotedar of his own caste.
Responsible for Phulbari and Patiram with Kali Sarkar; one of two peasant members of the first Dinajpur district party committee.

text.role: Peasant leader, Phulbari (Dinajpur); member of the Bengal Legislative Assembly from 1946
text.summaryCard: A peasant leader from Phulbari in Dinajpur, elected to the Bengal Legislative Assembly in 1946 as the peasants' own candidate, who led the Tebhaga struggle in his area.
text.fullEntry: Rupnarayan Roy was a peasant leader of the Phulbari area with some schooling, who built up the Krishak Samiti in several parts of Dinajpur district. In the 1946 Legislative Assembly election the Krishak Samiti and the Communist Party put him up as a candidate from the peasantry itself, and he defeated a jotedar candidate of his own caste. He was one of two peasant members of the first Dinajpur district committee of the Communist Party, and during Tebhaga shared responsibility for the Phulbari and Patiram areas with Kali Sarkar.

entries.why: The old text was a placeholder.
entries.note: Tebhaga Sankhya (scan p. 89) names the first adhiar elected to the Assembly from Dinajpur as 'Rupnarayan Sarkar' and says he was killed in 1973. The surname differs from every other mention, so the 1973 death is left out until confirmed.

add.supports: A provincial peasant leader sent by the provincial committee to Jalpaiguri to look into the local proposal to launch Tebhaga; approved the start after a survey of support among peasants.
Cited with Bhabani Sen and Mani Singh for later self-criticism of the movement's weaknesses.

text.summaryCard: A provincial Kisan Sabha leader sent to Jalpaiguri to decide whether the Tebhaga struggle should start there, who gave the go-ahead after a survey of peasant support.
text.fullEntry: When the Jalpaiguri district committee asked to launch the Tebhaga struggle, the provincial committee sent Krishnavinod Roy to investigate. He met peasant leaders from Boda, Pachagarh and Debiganj and gave permission to begin only after they had counted support among peasants in each area. He is also cited, with Bhabani Sen and Mani Singh, for later self-criticism of the movement's weaknesses.

add.supports: Known as Patal Babu; an organiser of the railway workers' union formed in 1938; general secretary of the Dooars tea workers' union; named among the leaders of Tebhaga in the Dooars, described by a participant as mainly an Adivasi movement.

text.role: Trade union and Tebhaga leader, Dooars (Jalpaiguri)
text.summaryCard: Known as Patal Babu, a railway and tea workers' organiser in the Dooars who was among the leaders of Tebhaga there.
text.fullEntry: Debaprasad Ghosh, known as Patal Babu, organised railway workers in the Dooars from 1938, moving through gang quarters along the line and into the tea gardens nearby, and became general secretary of the tea workers' union formed at Malbazar. A participant's memoir names him first among the leaders of the Tebhaga movement in the Dooars, which it describes as mainly an Adivasi movement.

add.supports: Leader of the Tebhaga struggle in Narail, Jessore; himself a small jotedar with about 30 bighas; a Muslim peasant leader in an area where most of the movement's fighters were Namasudra cultivators.

text.summaryCard: Leader of the Tebhaga struggle in Narail, Jessore, who was himself a small landholder and sided with his own sharecroppers.
text.fullEntry: Noor Jalal led the Tebhaga struggle in the Narail area of Jessore district. He was himself a small jotedar with about thirty bighas, and went against his own and his family's interest in backing the sharecroppers under him. Most of the movement's fighters in the area were Namasudra cultivators, alongside Muslim peasants, and attempts were made there to turn the struggle into a Hindu-Muslim quarrel.

add.supports: His own account of jotedars and their staff leaving Kakdwip and of firing from a landlord's office; remembered with 'Ahalya ma' as a hero of the Tebhaga struggle.

text.summaryCard: A leader of the Tebhaga struggle in Kakdwip in the Sundarbans, whose own account of it survives.
text.fullEntry: Kansari Halder was a leader of the Tebhaga struggle in Kakdwip in the 24 Parganas Sundarbans. His written account describes jotedars and their agents leaving Kakdwip for Calcutta and Midnapore, and firing on peasants from a landlord's office. Writers for the movement's fiftieth anniversary named him, with Ahalya of Chandanpiri, among the heroes of Tebhaga.

add.supports: His account of women's armed action at Nandigram-Mohammadpur and Chak Gopal in Midnapore, and of settlements in which cultivators kept 60 per cent.

text.summaryCard: A Tebhaga leader in Midnapore whose account records women's armed resistance around Nandigram.
text.fullEntry: Bhupal Panda's account of the Tebhaga movement in Midnapore describes peasant women at Nandigram-Mohammadpur confronting police and landlords' men, naming Bimala Maji, and women driving off a police party at Chak Gopal. It also records that many landlords were forced into compromises leaving 60 per cent of the crop to the cultivators.

add.supports: Secretary of the Burdwan district committee of the undivided CPI, 1939-49; 'a leading figure' of the Tebhaga movement; president of the All India Kisan Sabha; oversaw land reform in West Bengal.
Minister of Land and Land Reforms from 1977; sharecroppers' tenure secured under him.

Transported to the Andaman Cellular Jail at 18; peasant leader first in Burdwan; Minister for Land and Land Revenue in the 1967 United Front government; General Secretary of the All India Kisan Sabha; died July 1974.
